summary: First English narrative for the 13-14 September 2008 decision to let Lehman Brothers fail, written from the case's primary-source facts (FCIC Final Report Chapter 18 and quoted testimony; Wallison's FCIC dissent; Ball, NBER WP 22410).

narrative.hook: It is Sunday, 14 September 2008. The deal to sell Lehman Brothers has just collapsed in London, and if the firm has no money by Monday morning it files for bankruptcy. Do you put public money behind it, or let it go?
narrative.short_setup: Lehman Brothers had lost heavily on real estate, and during the week of 8 September a run by its counterparties drained its cash. On Friday night Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke and New York Fed President Timothy Geithner gathered Wall Street's chief executives at the New York Fed. Paulson told them a private-sector solution was the only option. By Saturday night it seemed to have worked: Barclays would buy Lehman, and a consortium of banks would finance its worst assets. Then, on Sunday morning, Barclays reported that Britain's Financial Services Authority would not approve the deal. Bank of America, the other possible buyer, had agreed to buy Merrill Lynch instead. Six months earlier the Fed had lent to help JP Morgan buy Bear Stearns, and the rescue had been fiercely criticised. Now the officials had hours to decide whether the government would step in.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The case for stepping in was the danger of a disorderly failure. On Saturday, Lehman's lawyers had given the Fed a document warning that its default would 'trigger a cascade of defaults' through subsidiaries with large derivatives books. Paulson himself had told the bankers on Friday that a sudden wind-down could cause a precipitous drop in asset prices, collateral calls and reduced liquidity, which is to say systemic risk. There was a precedent: in March the Fed had used its emergency lending powers to support the sale of Bear Stearns, and those powers required only that loans be secured to the Reserve Bank's satisfaction, not fully secured. Lending Lehman enough to open on Monday might buy time for an orderly sale or wind-down instead of a crash.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for refusing was about money, law and precedent. The Fed could not inject capital into a firm or give guarantees; it could only lend, and only with a reasonable expectation of being repaid. If Lehman was short of good collateral and the run continued, a loan might simply be lost while the firm failed anyway. The rescue of Bear Stearns had brought heavy criticism, and participants told investigators that a Lehman rescue had been described more than once as politically very difficult. Rescuing a second large firm in six months also risked teaching markets that none would ever be allowed to fail. And Lehman's troubles had been public for months: perhaps markets had had time to prepare.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: The government refused. Paulson held to the position that there would be no public money; New York Fed General Counsel Tom Baxter later told the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission that Paulson had made clear there would be 'not a penny'. On Sunday morning a Treasury official emailed that the U.S. government was 'united behind no money' and that there was 'no way in hell Paulson could blink now'. A Fed guarantee to replace Barclays' was, for Paulson, unequivocally out of the question. A last appeal by Paulson to the British Chancellor, Alistair Darling, failed. Without a buyer or support, Lehman Brothers Holdings filed for bankruptcy at 1:45 a.m. on Monday 15 September.
narrative.outcome_story: Lehman's failure triggered default clauses in derivatives contracts across its subsidiaries, and its bankruptcy counsel later called it 'the largest, most complex, multi-faceted and far-reaching bankruptcy case ever filed in the United States'. Within days the Fed made an emergency loan to rescue the insurer AIG, and the following week Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley became bank holding companies. Many economists came to believe that the bankruptcy greatly worsened the financial crisis and the recession that followed. Lehman was the only large financial institution to go bankrupt during the crisis.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
It is easy to say the government should obviously have saved Lehman, given what followed. That is outcome talking. Nobody knows what would have happened if it had been rescued: the economist Laurence Ball, who argues it could and should have been, says himself that Lehman might have survived, been sold, or wound down. The fair question is whether the decision was well made on what was known that Sunday.

The constraints were real. The Fed had no power to inject capital, and lending into a run against weak collateral could have lost taxpayers a great deal without saving the firm. The political backlash over Bear Stearns was real, and so was the worry about teaching markets that every big firm would be rescued.

But the record of how the decision was made is weak. Bernanke later told the FCIC that the Fed had no legal choice because Lehman lacked collateral, yet days after the bankruptcy he had given a different explanation, that markets had had time to prepare. The FCIC noted that the Fed furnished no written analysis showing Lehman's collateral was insufficient. Ball, after going through the record, found no evidence that collateral adequacy was examined before the bankruptcy and concluded that the decision was made primarily by Paulson. Lehman's own lawyers had warned of a cascade of defaults. And within days the Fed rescued AIG. A decision whose stated basis was not documented at the time, and was substantially reversed within the week, scores poorly on process.

There is also a deeper argument that has nothing to do with legal authority. Peter Wallison, a dissenting member of the FCIC, argued that the rescue of Bear Stearns had taught markets to expect rescue, so that letting Lehman fail six months later shocked them precisely because it broke that expectation. On his view the error was the inconsistency between the two decisions. Whichever account is right, the lesson is the same: the expectations you create with one decision become part of the situation in the next.
narrative.decision_principle: If you may later need to explain that you had no choice, do the analysis that would show it before you decide, not after; and remember that the expectations your previous decisions created are part of the risk you are managing now.
narrative.longform_story:
On Friday night, 12 September 2008, the chief executives of Wall Street's biggest firms were summoned to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Waiting for them were the Treasury Secretary, Henry Paulson, the Fed chairman, Ben Bernanke, and the president of the New York Fed, Timothy Geithner. The subject was Lehman Brothers.

Lehman had lost heavily on real estate. During the week just ending, the firms that lent it money and traded with it had pulled back, and its cash had drained away. Unless something changed over the weekend, it would not be able to open for business on Monday.

Paulson set out the terms. A private-sector solution, he said, was the only option. A sudden, disorderly wind-down could cause a precipitous drop in asset prices, collateral calls and a squeeze on liquidity. The bankers in the room had to find a way to prevent that. The Fed would help with regulatory approvals and access to its lending facilities, but it would not provide 'any form of extraordinary credit support'. Tom Baxter, the New York Fed's general counsel, later told investigators that Paulson had made it clear there would be no government assistance: 'not a penny'.

Not everyone took that at face value. Lehman's lawyer, H. Rodgin Cohen, told the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission he thought the government was 'playing a game of chicken', hoping to push the private sector into taking on Lehman's liabilities. It had been said more than once, he recalled, that rescuing Lehman would be politically very difficult after the blowback over Bear Stearns. In March the Fed had lent to support JP Morgan's purchase of Bear, and the criticism had been intense.

On Saturday the bankers went through Lehman's assets and concluded they were overvalued. Merrill Lynch's chief executive, John Thain, decided that Lehman would fail and that Merrill would be next, and went to see Bank of America's Ken Lewis. By Sunday Bank of America had agreed to buy Merrill instead of Lehman. The same Saturday, Lehman's lawyers gave the Fed a document describing how Lehman's default would 'trigger a cascade of defaults' through subsidiaries with large derivatives books.

By Saturday night, though, it looked as if the worst had been avoided. Barclays would buy Lehman, with the consortium of banks financing the most troubled assets. A deal seemed close.

On Sunday morning, Barclays' chief executive and president told Paulson, Geithner and SEC Chairman Christopher Cox that Britain's Financial Services Authority had declined to approve it. The sticking point was a guarantee. The New York Fed required Barclays to guarantee Lehman's obligations until the deal closed, as JP Morgan had done for Bear Stearns. Under British law that needed a vote of Barclays' shareholders, which would take time, and the FSA would not waive the requirement. Geithner pleaded with the FSA's chairman; the FSA wanted the New York Fed to provide the guarantee instead. For Paulson, a Fed guarantee was out of the question. Paulson made a last appeal to the British Chancellor, Alistair Darling, without success. Two years later Darling said plainly that he had vetoed the deal. 'My first reaction', he recalled, 'was "If this is such a good deal how come no American bank is going to go near it?"'

That left the officials with the decision this story is about. They could provide public support to keep Lehman alive long enough for an orderly sale or wind-down, or they could let it file for bankruptcy.

The argument for support was the cascade. Lehman was wired into the financial system through derivatives and short-term funding, and no one could map what its sudden failure would do. The argument against was money, law and precedent. The Fed could lend but not inject capital or give guarantees, and it could lend only with a reasonable expectation of repayment. A second rescue after Bear Stearns would tell every large firm that it would be saved. That morning a Treasury official wrote in an email that the government was 'united behind no money' and that there was 'no way in hell Paulson could blink now'.

There was no blink. At 1:45 a.m. on Monday 15 September, Lehman Brothers Holdings filed for bankruptcy. Its failure triggered default clauses in derivatives contracts across its subsidiaries. Its bankruptcy counsel called it the largest, most complex and far-reaching bankruptcy case ever filed in the United States. Within days the Fed made an emergency loan to rescue the insurer AIG, and the next week Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley became bank holding companies. Lehman was the only large financial institution to go bankrupt during the crisis, and many economists came to believe its failure greatly worsened the crisis and the recession that followed.

Why it was allowed to fail is still argued over. Bernanke told the FCIC that the Fed had no choice: Lehman did not have enough collateral to support a loan big enough to meet the run, and lending anyway would only have saddled taxpayers with losses. The commission pointed out that days after the bankruptcy he had given a different reason, that markets had had time to prepare, and that the Fed had furnished no written analysis showing the collateral was inadequate. In 2016 the economist Laurence Ball concluded that the Fed did have the authority to lend, that the record showed no examination of Lehman's collateral before the bankruptcy, and that the decision was made primarily by Paulson. Lehman's former chief executive insisted it had had the collateral and needed only a bridge. Inside the Fed, some policymakers argued that letting Lehman fail was the only way to make credible the idea that no firm was too big to fail. And Peter Wallison, one of the FCIC's dissenting commissioners, argued that the real error was the inconsistency: having rescued Bear Stearns and taught markets to expect rescue, the government then let a larger firm fail.

Nobody can know what a rescue would have led to. What the record does show is a decision taken under real constraints, with a stated basis that was not documented at the time, and reversed in substance within the week. The question it leaves is less about Lehman than about how to decide when every choice is a precedent.
